title: The Drosophila escape motor circuit shows differential vulnerability to aging linked to functional decay.
source_locator: Results, section 'Localizing the neural correlates for aging-related loss of escape behavior' (text after Fig 8 legend); Fig 4A-4B; Methods 'Optogenetically-induced escape response'
quote: escape responses can be elicited by a 50 ms red-light flash with ≥80% response probability throughout adult life (Fig 4A, red bars)
mapping_basis: Paper calls the neuron the giant fiber descending neuron (GF) and labels it 'GF or DNp01' (Fig 3A legend); GF is a listed synonym of DNp01 in synonyms.csv, mapping to one MANC type.
stimulation: Red light 594 nm; Methods: three 2 s pulses every 10 s; Results text says a 50 ms red-light flash
sensory_condition: single fly in 9 x 2 cm Petri dish under dim infrared illumination
penetrance: >=80% of flies escaped at all ages (~95-99% up to 60 d, ~80% at >60 d); ~50% of >60 d visual non-responders (Fig 4B); 0% of UAS-GFP controls
n_flies_note: Fig 4A test groups n = 167, 158, 147, 134, 118 across age bins (724 total); Fig 4B n = 33 non-responders (legend), figure shows (23); controls 136-192 per age bin, 36 in Fig 4B
notes: Escape is described in the paper as a jump followed by flight (single movement, so all leg-rhythm fields are no); escape scored by eye from an infrared camera, legs not tracked. The paper calls the driver 'GF descending neuron'-specific split-GAL4 ('highly specific'); expression assumed bilateral (two GFs) but not stated. Sex: Methods say male flies were removed for experimental testing, so males likely. Stimulus discrepancy: 50 ms flash in Results vs 2 s pulses in Methods. Fig 4A (age series) and Fig 4B (pre-selected old visual non-responders) coded as one record (same line, preparation and outcome). Electrical GF stimulation (SLR/TTM recordings) not coded (not opto/thermogenetic; no observed leg movement).
